The models in earlier chapters assumed that the outcomes
$Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ were mutually independent given the covariates.
Many epidemiologic studies collect data in **clusters**:
repeated measurements on the same person,
patients treated at the same hospital,
or houses in the same county
[@dobson4e, Chapter 11].
Observations in the same cluster
tend to resemble one another more than observations in different clusters,
so the independence assumption fails.
Ignoring that correlation usually makes standard errors too small,
because the data carry less information
than the same number of independent observations would
[@dobson4e, Chapter 11].

Two kinds of model term describe clusters.

{{< include _subfiles/intro-multilevel-models/_def-random-effect.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-fixed-vs-random}
#### Fixed versus random effects

- In a trial comparing a new drug with a placebo,
the treatment groups are the only two groups of interest,
so treatment is a fixed effect.
- In a study that measures each of 20 patients several times,
the 20 patients are a sample from the population of all patients,
and we want conclusions that apply to patients beyond these 20,
so patient is a random effect.
:::

Random effects can be **nested** or **crossed**.
Effects are nested when each lower-level group belongs to exactly one higher-level group,
such as batches within laboratories.
Effects are crossed when every level of one factor can appear with every level of the other,
such as patients and raters when every rater scores every patient
[@rocke2021epi204].

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include _subfiles/intro-multilevel-models/_def-mixed-model.qmd >}}

The same ideas extend from linear models to logistic and Poisson regression
[@rocke2021epi204].
